19672-the-holladay-case:
Burton E. Stevenson was an American writer of mystery and adventure stories. The Holladay Case is one of his detective tales. It opens in a law office thrown into alarm. A junior clerk named Royce bursts in, shaken and distracted. He carries a newspaper that has clearly stunned him. His employer Graham wheels from his desk in astonishment.

A shocked entrance promises a death or disgrace in the headlines. Stevenson liked legal settings, secrets, and patient unraveling. His detectives work through talk, papers, and close observation. The opening puts all three in play within a page. Readers who like early American detective fiction will find the period machinery here.
19945-bakemono-yashiki-the-haunted-house:
Bakemono Yashiki means the haunted house, or goblin house, in Japanese. James de Benneville retold it from Japanese sources. Like its companion volumes, it leans on Edo maps of 1857 and 1866. Street plans from the Go Edo Zusetsu Shuran fill out the setting. A haunted house needs a real address to chill properly. De Benneville supplies Edo in detail around his ghosts.

Bakemono are shape-changing beings of Japanese folklore. Tales about them blend terror with sly humor. De Benneville collected such stories while living in Japan. His retellings introduced many Western readers to Japanese ghost lore. The topographical fussiness is part of his charm. Haunting, here, is a matter of record.
20085-the-tragic-muse:
Henry James published The Tragic Muse, a novel about art, theatre, and English society. James writes of a race whose energy strikes foreign eyes with force. Some feel awe at it, others feel sharp dislike instead. That cool, exact eye marks the whole book from the start.

The tragic muse is the stage muse, and acting drives the tale. A young woman must weigh art against the safe life society offers. James traces small shifts of mind with great care and depth. Readers get one of his rich studies of ambition, love, and the price of art.
20511-the-little-mother-goose:
The Little Mother Goose, published in 1912, gathers the classic nursery rhymes for very young children. It presents them with pictures in color and in black and white. The rhymes are the ones English-speaking children have learned for centuries.

Here is the old riddle rhyme of the road to St. Ives. As I was going to St. Ives, I met a man with seven wives. Every wife had seven sacks, every sack had seven cats, and every cat had seven kits. Generations of children have puzzled over how many were going to St. Ives.
20767-the-life-of-mansie-wauch-tailor-in:
Mansie Wauch, a tailor in Dalkeith, tells his own life in broad Scots. He recalls his grandfather, a tall old man with white locks and rose-red cheeks. Blind with age, the old man still sits clear in the boy's early memory.

David Macbeth Moir wrote this famed Scots tale of small-town life. Mansie bumbles, boasts, and repents through work, love, and local fame. The dialect gives the book its warmth and much of its fun. Readers meet a Scotland of kirks, fairs, and sharp tongues, seen through one vain but kind heart, drawn with love and gentle mockery.
20984-prudy-keeping-house:
Dotty with eyes like living diamonds watches a snowstorm as Prudy Keeping House opens. Prudy, fair and sweet, begs Horace to shut the window before the plants freeze. Sophie May peoples her tale with the famed Clarke children in bright strokes.

Prudy, the eldest girl, tries her hand at keeping house in this tale. Sophie May, whose real name was Rebecca Clarke, wrote the Prudy books for young girls. Dishes, guests, and small disasters test Prudy's young charge. The set charmed post-Civil War homes with its true talk, warm humour, and sisters drawn from life as their author knew it.
21217-the-one-moss-rose:
Leonard Dobbin, a poor labourer on Squire Courtenay's estate, keeps a humble cottage that is a pattern of neatness. The Reverend P. B. Power's 1872 story centres on Dobbin's one luxury, his little flower garden. The pride of that garden is a moss-rose tree.

The rose belongs in a special way to Dobbin's crippled little son Jacob. He watches it from the window and creeps out when he can to water it and pick off snails. No mother, the story says, watched a baby more eagerly than Jacob watched his rose. Power builds a gentle moral tale around the flower and the boy.
21317-a-life-s-eclipse:
John Grange, an under-gardener on Mrs Mostyn's estate, loves Mary Ellis, the bailiff's daughter. Her father James Ellis is angry that a mere gardener dares think of her. George Manville Fenn then drops a tree on John's ambitions: sent up a great cedar to tidy a broken bough, he falls on his head.

John recovers from the concussion blind. His rival Daniel Barnett takes the head gardener's post John might have had. Barnett plays cruel tricks on him, though blind John still works well by touch. When John vanishes without trace, rumour accuses Barnett of making away with him. Fenn saves the truth for a surprise ending.
21358-the-ocean-cat-s-paw-the-story-of-a:
Rodd, a Devon boy fishing a Dartmoor stream, hides a young Frenchman who has just escaped from the Dartmoor prison camp of the Napoleonic Wars. George Manville Fenn then sends Rodd's uncle to sea on a government grant. The uncle, a doctor and natural history researcher, is to buy a ship and collect specimens. Rodd sails with him.

Bad weather drives them into a French port, and later they meet a strange brig holed below the waterline in a fight. Her officers prove to be the escaped boy and his father, a count. British seamanship patches the hole. The strange cruise of the title ranges far beyond one act of boyish mercy.
21446-favourite-fables-in-prose-and-vers:
Favourite Fables, in prose and verse, was printed in London in 1870 with drawings by Harrison Weir. The set opens with the fox and the goat, where a fox falls into a well. He swims from side to side and cannot climb out by his own pains.

Twenty-four pictures back a run of short, famed tales for the young. Readers meet the frog and the ox, the dove and the ant, and the frogs who wanted a king. Other fables treat the fox without a tail and the horse and the stag. Each ends with its lesson plainly drawn, in the old manner.
21541-quiet-please:
Groverzb wants only peace and quiet in Kevin Scott's short tale Quiet Please, from Worlds of If in November 1961. He is willing to scream his head off to get it, as the blurb jokes. A big porter lugs his piano in and warns him he will not like the planet.

The natives stand no more than three feet tall and never talk aloud. That silence is just why Groverzb, who loathes conversation, has come. His house is a gutted block once home to the Little People. By evening a violet glow falls, small folk dash below, and no voice breaks the calm he craves.
21618-the-aztec-treasure-house:
Thomas Allibone Janvier hunts Montezuma's gold in The Aztec Treasure-House, copyrighted in 1890. A verse at the front promises marvels, hidden gold, and gallant fights. Fray Antonio and a dying cacique hold the first clues to the hoard.

A monk's manuscript and Montezuma's messenger guide the seekers into Mexico. Chapters pass a submerged city, a swinging statue, and a cave of the dead. The Chac-Mool stair and a temple in the clouds raise the stakes. Janvier, who lived in Mexico and loved its lore, packs the tale with real learning worn lightly throughout.
21740-the-iron-horse:
Trains shake the house where little Gertie lives in this Ballantyne tale of the railways. Her father, John Marrot, is an engine driver, and the passing trains rattle her bed curtains day and night. Gertie is six, rosy, and sweet, with a mind very much her own. She saves her kisses for a chosen few, her father first among them.

Ballantyne researched the railways as he did each trade he wrote about. The tale shows engine crews, their homes, their risks, and their pride in the iron horse. Domestic warmth and real danger share the chapters. It gives young readers a close, kind look at the men who ran the steam age.
21746-the-lighthouse:
Two fishermen row out from Forfarshire on a still summer morning at the start of this Ballantyne tale. The sea lies like glass, and the big, rough-spoken boatman jokes that the calm will help them land on the rock. That rock, far from shore, is where a lighthouse must rise. The work ahead will test builders, sailors, and engineers alike.

Ballantyne tells how such lights were built on wave-washed rocks at the start of the nineteenth century. He mixes the building work with the lives of the men who did it. Storms fight the work at every stage. The finished light stands as proof of patience, skill, and plain courage.
21998-the-lion-s-mouse:
A hard man is caught in a net of his own making in The Lion's Mouse, a 1919 novel by C. N. and A. M. Williamson. Roger Sands has steel-gray eyes, brows drawn low and nearly meeting, and an aggressive clean-shaven chin. He has the air of being hard as nails. Then a young and beautiful woman hovers at his door, breathing perfume, and begs him to help her.

The contents run in fable order: the lion, the net, the mouse. The queen's pearls, a parcel with gold seals, a bluff that failed and a bluff that won fill the middle. Murder and a brown trunk darken the later chapters. The Williamsons wrote sleek society thrillers as a husband-and-wife team. This one turns Aesop's fable into a romance of rescue.
22246-the-upper-berth-by-the-waters-of-p:
Two long tales by F. Marion Crawford share this volume: The Upper Berth and By the Waters of Paradise. Crawford, an American novelist who lived in Italy, wrote ghost stories of rare polish. The Upper Berth is his most famous. A traveller shares a stateroom with something that will not stay dead, and the ship's officers must be convinced cabin by cabin.

The narrator of the second tale recalls a dinner conversation so boring it would have bored Prometheus on his rock. From that frame the paradise story unfolds. Crawford's horror is quiet, seamanlike, and exact. The Upper Berth still sails through anthologies as one of the finest sea-ghost stories ever written.
22265-frank-merriwell-s-cruise:
Frank Merriwell's Cruise belongs to the dime-novel series that made Frank Merriwell America's model schoolboy. Street and Smith published the tale in 1898, in the Merriwell stories written chiefly by Gilbert Patten. A well-dressed youth pays his cabbie silently and walks into a hotel. A boy takes his bag; he steps to the clerk's desk and speaks, and the adventure is under way.

Merriwell's cruise takes him by yacht into scrapes, rescues, and sporting contests. He never drinks, never swears, and never loses his temper or a game that matters. Millions of boys followed his cruises and campaigns. This number is pure Merriwell: clean, brisk, and perfectly sure of its hero.
22418-dollars-and-sense:
Colonel W. C. Hunter wrote Dollars and Sense, published in 1908. It is a book of business counsel for working readers. Hunter promises a welcome to those who are square, ambitious, and patient.

These chapters, he says, will be old friends to such readers. A few minutes or a few hours both serve for reading. Readers may return as often as they wish, he adds. Each return visit will impress some new truth, he promises. The book belongs to the self-help shelf of its decade. Its lessons join money sense to character and patience. Modern readers get period business advice in a bluff, friendly voice.
22474-fringilla-some-tales-in-verse:
Richard Doddridge Blackmore wrote Fringilla, some tales in verse. Blackmore, the novelist of Lorna Doone, here turns to rhymed storytelling. One tale gives a curious legend on the origin of jealousy.

When Adam and Eve lived in Paradise, the tale begins, Adam withdrew at evening. He retired to the garden's recesses for prayer each night. On one occasion, the Devil appeared to Eve alone. Her solitude, he claimed, was owed to another fair one. Eve replied that it could not possibly be so. She was, she noted, the only woman in existence. That neat logic gives the legend its dry, comic bite.
22657-steam-its-generation-and-use:
Steam: Its Generation and Use is a handbook of steam engineering, first issued by a leading boiler maker and kept in print for decades; this entry holds the 1919 edition. The catalog record names no author. In the steam age, such a book sat in every power plant, part textbook and part company catalog.

The front matter lists offices from Adelaide to St. Petersburg, a map of world industry in itself. Inside, engineers found the physics of heat, the chemistry of boiler water, and rules for safe, thrifty firing. The book taught a trade as much as it sold boilers. It remains a standard period source on how the world made power before electricity took over.
22820-the-crooked-house:
Brandon Fleming's 1921 mystery novel The Crooked House opens with a fright on a dim street. The Right Honorable John Tranter turns, latch-key in hand, as an enormous figure slips noiselessly from the shadow of the next house. The figure's sheer size, grotesque in the lamplight, startles Tranter back.

From that eerie meeting, Fleming builds a tale of crime and pursuit in postwar London. Tranter and the giant stranger stand at the heart of the puzzle, and the crooked house of the title gathers the threads. The writing favors atmosphere, sudden reveals, and cliff-edge chapter ends. Readers who like Golden Age detection in a popular, fast-moving vein will find the machinery they expect, well oiled.
22872-susan-clegg-and-a-man-in-the-house:
Anne Warner's Susan Clegg had lived alone since her father's death, and not unhappily. She had been a good daughter while she had a parent to live with, and she kept her small household in her own firm way. Then, as the title promises, a man comes into the house, and her settled routine meets its test.

Warner built a small comic world around Susan and her friend Mrs. Latham, whose talk carries much of the fun. Dialect, gossip, and stubborn common sense drive these stories more than plot does. The 1906 volume continues a popular series of the day. Readers who enjoy gentle village comedy, told largely in conversation, will feel at home in Susan's parlor.
23030-buying-a-horse:
A friend goes horse shopping in Buying a Horse, a comic sketch of the turf. He walked home encouraged, the narrator says, his purpose seeming less monstrous to a hardened offender in such matters. He began announcing it boldly, claiming he would not go above a hundred, which was not true. Prudence, in his private accounting, meant stretching to a hundred and twenty-five only when driven to it.

Every horse buyer knows that extremity. The sketch follows the bargaining, the vets, the friends with advice, and the horse world's cheerful traps for the earnest novice. Its humor depends on small dishonesties everyone commits. Written when horses still filled the streets, it reads now as both a joke and a document, a field guide to a vanished marketplace.
23037-stories-in-verse:
A flower seller haunts Stories in Verse. One poem fixes its gaze on a flower seller and holds her fast. Lovely as she is, the great town is devouring her in its noise and struggle. How poverty grinds down a life, the poet asks, for what is a beautiful face in the slime of a city?

Verse tales of street life fill this collection of narrative poems. Its subjects are the city's casualties and charmers, told in rhymes meant to be felt quickly. Sentiment was the point, and the poems deliver it without embarrassment. The book preserves the popular poetry of the parlor and the newspaper column, where a flower girl could carry a whole evening's meditation on wealth and beauty.
23069-janet-mclaren-the-faithful-nurse:
Janet McLaren takes charge in Janet McLaren, the Faithful Nurse. The chapter summary tells her work plainly. Janet moves into a small town attic with the children and works to keep them all. Donald and David, the two boys, she manages to place at school. Her anxiety centers on Margaret's education.

An orphaned household held together by a servant's devotion gives this tale its heart. Janet nurses, earns, plans, and sacrifices in the approved manner of the improving story, yet the labor described is real labor. Scottish settings and Presbyterian conscience stiffen the sentiment. Readers get a period portrait of the faithful nurse as a type, drawn with admiration that modern eyes can share while questioning its terms.
23096-and-judas-iscariot-together-with-o:
Two thieves divide eternity in And Judas Iscariot, a set of evangelistic addresses published in 1906. One thief, the preacher says, let grace do its full work and won Christ's pardon. The other knew remorse but never repentance, and shut grace out. One became a mighty preacher. The other's crime still horrifies every reader.

Judas stands as the warning at the sermons' center, remorse mistaken for repentance. John Wilbur Chapman, the era's leading evangelist, built such addresses for mass revival meetings, and their structure shows it, contrast, urgency, appeal. The accompanying addresses work the same ground. Readers meet American revival preaching in its professional prime.
23135-history-of-circumcision-from-the-e:
Doctors form a class of their own in this History of Circumcision from the earliest times to the present. The operation, the author notes, went beyond the intellectual class. Doctors themselves form such a class across America, France, and England, he reports. Among medical families, he has personally found the practice observed by every male member, as a guard for health.

Peter Charles Remondino, the San Diego physician to whom the work is credited, surveys the rite across religions, climates, and centuries. His chapters mix anthropology, scripture, and medical argument in the confident manner of 1891. The book helped spread the era's medical case for the operation in America. Read now, it is a period document twice over, in its facts and in its certainties alike.
23144-the-war-trail-the-hunt-of-the-wild:
Thomas Mayne Reid rhapsodizes in The War Trail, the hunt of the wild horse. Reid greets Anahuac, old Mexico, like a lover returning. His fancy carries him back to its shores, its broad savannahs, and the shade of its corozo palms. Even his horse, he swears, neighs with joy at the scene.

Mexico's plains, mustangs, and war paths fill Reid's romance at full gallop. He climbs mountains of porphyry in the same breath, toward crags of quartz yielding white silver and yellow gold. Reid's prose was always half the adventure, purple, learned, and in love with the land it crossed. The hunt of the wild horse gives that prose its perfect subject.
23196-songs-for-a-little-house:
Christopher Morley published Songs for a Little House in 1917, a book of poems about home and daily life. One poem follows workers down Thirty-second Street at day's end. Their feet seem to chant homeward as they tramp, footsore and weary, yet stirred anew by the walk.

Nightfall makes up for the day: the ringing telephones stop, and golden train windows cast brightness on the snow. Morley writes plain city scenes with warmth and a light touch. Readers get short, musical poems that find comfort in streets, trains, and the small house waiting at the end of the day.
a-legend-of-montrose:
Walter Scott set his novel during the Scottish civil wars of the 1640s, when the Marquis of Montrose raised the Highlands for the King. Scott's introduction says the tale centers on the sad fate of young Lord Kilpont and on James Stewart of Ardvoirlich, the man whose hand struck him down. Feuds between great families open the story.

The main text follows soldiers and Highlanders through camps and marches, with the talkative soldier Dugald Dalgetty among its best-loved figures. Appendices add Clan Alpin's Vow and The Children of the Mist, with Scott's notes. Battles, loyalty, and clan hatred drive a compact, stirring piece of Scottish history in fiction.
an-anthology-of-australian-verse:
Bertram Stevens edited this gathering of Australian poets, writing the introduction himself. The contents begin with William Charles Wentworth and Charles Harpur, early voices of the colony. They run through Sir Henry Parkes and Rolf Boldrewood. They end with Adam Lindsay Gordon, whose Sick Stock-rider became a bush classic. Henry Kendall's Leaves from Australian Forests and Songs from the Mountains appear in force.

The poems sing of drought, floods, horses, shearing sheds, and the strange light of the bush, beside love lyrics and city verse. Stevens aimed to show that a young country had already made a literature. The anthology served for years as the standard doorway into Australian poetry.
as-a-matter-of-course:
Annie Payson Call published As a Matter of Course in 1894 as a handbook for calming the nerves. Call, already known for Power Through Repose, aims to remove nervous irritants from daily life. Her preface says such irritants cause disease and spoil usefulness and pleasure. The governing image is a stone in the traveller's path.

Call argues that small obstacles should be stepped over as a matter of course, without fretting. Chapters treat physical care, amusements, brain impressions, and the triviality of trivialities. Others handle moods, tolerance, sympathy, children, and illness. She distinguishes sentiment from sentimentality near the close. The book belongs to the New Thought movement, which taught mental habits as a path to health, and it still reads as gentle, practical psychology.
at-the-villa-rose:
A. E. W. Mason's At the Villa Rose is a detective novel of the French Riviera and Geneva. Mr. Ricardo, a rich widower approaching fifty, takes his annual cure at Aix-les-Bains. He pretends to take the waters and plays baccarat at the Villa des Fleurs. Inspector Hanaud of the Paris Sûreté is holidaying nearby.

A cry for help draws Ricardo into the murder of Madame Dauvray at her villa. Her companion Celia disappears, and her maid Hélène Vauquier gives evidence. Chapters pursue an unopened letter, an aluminium flask, and a séance. Hanaud explains at the close, gathering the threads in Geneva and Aix. Mason writes polished fair-play detection, with Ricardo as the bewildered amateur beside the great detective. The novel helped define the country-house mystery between the wars of crime fiction.
boris-godunov-a-drama-in-verse:
Alexander Pushkin's Boris Godunov, rendered into English verse by Alfred Hayes, dramatizes Russia's time of troubles. The cast list names Boris, afterwards Tsar, with Princes Shuisky and Vorotinsky at his court. Father Pimen, an old monk and chronicler, keeps the record. Gregory Otrepiev, a young monk, will become the Pretender.

The play opens in the Kremlin palace in February 1598, as Boris hesitates to accept the crown. Pimen's cell reveals the murder of the Tsarevich Dimitry, the secret on which Boris's reign is built. Gregory flees to Poland, takes Dimitry's name, and wins Marina Mnishek's ambition. Armies, taverns, and battlefields carry the short scenes onward. Pushkin wrote in Shakespeare's chronicle manner, letting the people themselves judge their tsar. It remains Russia's great historical drama.
brentano-die-drei-nusse:
Three nuts, each holding a wonder and a test, drive Brentano's fairy tale Die drei Nuesse, given here in German. The hero's fortune turns on what the nuts conceal and when he dares to open them. Folk tradition supplies the bones; Brentano's Romantic richness supplies the flesh.

Small as the tale is, it shows a master working magic in the briefest compass. Wishes, dangers, and rewards arrive in classic fairy-tale rhythm. The German text lets readers savor his musical prose directly. Brentano could fill a paragraph with more enchantment than others manage in a chapter. The story makes a perfect short sample of his art for new readers.
bulchevy-s-book-of-english-verse:
Arthur Quiller-Couch edited this great anthology of English verse, issued here under a generic title because the Oxford name was a trademark. Quiller-Couch arranged the poems by author in time order, beginning with anonymous songs from about 1250. Chaucer and Hoccleve appear early; the book runs on to poets born in the later nineteenth century.

His preface explains the choices: the best poems, whole where possible, in the order English poetry grew. Ballads, lyrics, odes, and dramatic verse stand side by side. Generations of readers met English poetry through this single shelf-sized volume. It works still as a map of the tradition, generous in range and firm in taste.
captain-fracasse:
Theophile Gautier's Captain Fracasse follows the ruined young Baron de Sigognac, who leaves his decaying Castle Misery with a traveling theater troupe. The contents promise the Chariot of Thespis, brigands, a snowstorm, and the Blue Sun inn. Sigognac takes the stage name Captain Fracasse, a braggart soldier's part.

He falls for the actress Isabella while the Duke of Vallombreuse schemes to steal her, setting duels, abductions, and melees in motion. Gautier, who adored the theater, fills seventeenth-century France with players, swordsmen, and the gypsy girl Chiquita. The baron's first victory gives him confidence his enemy must now reckon with. Gautier's swashbuckler remains a French classic of romantic adventure.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-and-sch:
The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Clonmacnoise describes the abbey and school on the Shannon, halfway between Athlone and Banagher, as the most remarkable of Erin's ancient schools. Its founder, St. Ciaran, called Son of the Carpenter, chose a bleak region as better suited to followers of the Cross than the rich plains nearby.

Born at Fuerty in 512 and schooled by St. Finnian at Clonard, Ciaran joined the saintly youths later known as the Twelve Apostles of Erin. Finnian trusted the young Ciaran to teach and give out prayers in his absence, and would gladly have resigned his chair to keep him. The entry follows Ciaran's foundation and the school's fame among Ireland's monastic centres.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-melr:
The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Melrose describes an abbey in Roxburghshire, founded in 1136 by King David the First as Scotland's earliest Cistercian monastery. Its first community came from Rievaulx, and St. Mary's Abbey stood complete within ten years in a wide valley south of the Tweed.

English incursions ravaged Melrose repeatedly: Edward the Second's soldiers desecrated, pillaged and burned the church, and Richard the Second laid waste the country and fired the abbey in 1385. Through Robert the Bruce's generosity a statelier church began in 1326, cruciform and two hundred and fifty feet long, famed for the fairy lightness of its carvings and window tracery.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-newh:
The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Newhouse describes the first Premonstratensian abbey in England, near Brockelsby in Lincolnshire, founded in 1143 by Peter de Gousel. Peter acted with his lord Hugh de Bayeux's consent and Bishop Alexander of Lincoln's approbation, bringing a colony from Liegues Abbey near Calais under Abbot Henry.

William, Earl of Lincoln, hospitably received the White Canons and confirmed the gifts to Gelro, Newhouse's first abbot. Raised for Our Lady and St. Martial of Limoges, Newhouse became parent house to eleven English Premonstratensian houses. Granted to Charles, Duke of Suffolk, in Henry the Eighth's thirtieth year, only parts of its old foundations remain, and twenty-six abbots' names are known.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alessandro-fa:
The name Alessandro Farnese belongs to two cardinals, and this entry treats the younger. He was the son of Pier Luigi Farnese, first Duke of Parma, born in October 1520 and dead at Rome in February 1589. While a student at Bologna, he was made administrator of Parma in 1534. His uncle Paul III created him Cardinal-Deacon of Sant' Angelo that December and conferred offices and benefices on him.

Farnese was zealous for the poor and served the popes on legations and embassies, including a 1539 mission to Charles V and a 1545 embassy on the council. He accompanied papal troops against the Smalkald League in 1546 and stood as a candidate for the papacy in 1580. A promoter of the Tridentine reforms and a patron of literature, science, and art, he backed the architect Vignola for the Gesù in Rome and the palace at Caprarola. He was buried before the high altar of the Gesù.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-altar-of-repo:
The altar of repose, sometimes called sepulchre or tomb, more often repository, holds the Sacred Host consecrated at Holy Thursday Mass until Good Friday's Mass of the Presanctified. It must stand in the church, other than the altar where Mass is celebrated. Two hosts are consecrated on Holy Thursday. After the first is consumed, the second rests in a chalice covered with pall and inverted paten, under a white veil tied with ribbon, on the corporal until Mass ends.

The host is then borne in solemn procession to that altar of repose. It is kept in the tabernacle or an urn above the altar. Churches vie to adorn these altars and chapels with rich hangings, flowers, and lights, and Holy Thursday becomes a day of exceptional devotion. No mention of altar and procession appears before the late fifteenth century, earlier reservation having served Communion distribution, not the next day's service.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-altar-vase:
The Caeremoniale Episcoporum sanctions flowers between the candlesticks as certainly appropriate altar ornaments. Altar vases hold flowers decorating the altar, natural or artificial blooms set between the candlesticks as fitting ornaments for worship. Cut flowers, leaves, and ferns are meant here, rather than soil-potted plants, though potted plants may adorn the sanctuary around the altar.

Artificial flowers must use superior material and copy nature's variations faithfully and with some accuracy. Paper, cheap muslin, calico, and other inferior stuffs, and old or soiled flowers, are never allowed on the altar.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ancient-see-o: This 1913 reference piece on the ancient see of Odense — the bishopric of St. Canute's isle. Arthur Taylor tells its story. The martyr king fell in its church. The Reformation closed the old see. A vanished bishopric of Fyn. Its Canute shrine drew the pilgrims.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-anise: This 1913 reference article on anise — the biblical herb of the tithe. Edward Arbez notes its scriptural mention. The Pharisees tithed its tiny seeds. Christ rebuked their trifling care. A small herb of the Gospel. Its seeds flavor the Christmas cakes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-apocalypse: A 1913 entry on the Apocalypse — St. John's book of the last things. Christian Van den Biesen unfolds its visions. The Lamb conquers the beast. The Church reads it in hope. Scripture's most mysterious book. Its letters warn the seven churches.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-appeal-as-fro: This 1913 reference piece on the appel comme d'abus — the French appeal against church abuse. Richard Burtsell explains its Gallican use. The state checked the Church's courts. The Revolution swept it away. A weapon of the old regime. Its use vexed the Gallican bishops.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-apse: This 1913 reference article on the apse — the semicircular sanctuary. Thomas Poole traces its Roman roots. The bishop's throne stood in its curve. The basilicas kept the ancient form. The church's sacred head. Its vault glows with mosaic gold. Its conch holds the enthroned Christ.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-archdiocese: This 1913 reference piece on the archdiocese — the chief see of its province — sets out its place. The archbishop rules his own flock. The nearby bishops look to his chair. His church is the province's crown. The mother see of the region.

common-sense:
Thomas Paine, a recent English immigrant to America, fired the colonies toward independence with Common Sense in early 1776. Philadelphia readers passed the pamphlet hand to hand while war with Britain already burned. Paine argues in plain, hard sentences that America must cut loose from king and Parliament. His postscript of February 14, 1776 notes that no answer had yet appeared.

Four parts divide the case, starting with the origin and design of government in general. Paine separates society, born of human wants, from government, born of human wickedness. Monarchy and hereditary succession take a beating as absurd and insulting systems. Thoughts on the present state of American affairs then urge a clean break and a new union. A final section rates America's present ability, counting ships, men, and resources for war. Few pamphlets have moved a nation faster; readers still study Paine's mix of Bible talk, street logic, and moral heat.

Flint and Feather gathers the collected verse of E Pauline Johnson, the Canadian poet of Mohawk and English descent who performed her work across Canada and England. Johnson inscribed the book, by permission, to the Duke of Connaught as Head Chief of the Six Nations. A memorial introduction recalls her deathbed wish, her London recital tours of 1906, and a gratitude her friends describe as a passion rather than a sentiment.

What remains is the verse collection as Johnson shaped it, framed by those who knew her.

Baron d'Holbach's Good Sense, subtitled Freethoughts Opposed to Supernatural Ideas, is an English translation of his French Le Bon Sens. The undated translation names no translator, and a Bacon epigraph sets its theme: atheism leaves men to sense, philosophy and laws, while superstition erects an absolute monarchy in men's minds.

Contents ask what theology is, whether man is born with religious ideas, whether belief in God is necessary, and whether all religion is absurdity. Holbach argues plainly and polemically, in short chapters meant to be read and passed on. Readers interested in Enlightenment freethought will find Good Sense one of its bluntest, most readable statements.

govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_cyber-va:
In 1997 the Defense Department ran Eligible Receiver, an early classified exercise on cyber attack against the United States. This briefing book, posted in August 2018, draws on recently declassified documents and an NSA video. The exercise went well beyond computers, its papers show.

Testers staged mock terror attacks, hostage seizures, and special operations raids. Those physical scenes demonstrated how wide the damage from a cyber-domain attack could spread. The exercise is now called seminal because it woke senior officials to the threat. Its documents let readers see the moment American defense planning started taking cyber war seriously.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_foia_The: The Bolton Book Saga: Anatomy of a White House Cover-Up - the National Security Archive briefing-book page capture. The archivists capture, complete. A single capture. Dated material. From the archive's collection, for researchers and readers.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_nuclear-: In 1958 the United States and China fought a crisis over Taiwan and its offshore islands, and American planners weighed nuclear weapons in that fight. This briefing-book page revisits the 1958 Taiwan Strait Crisis as modern tensions over Taiwan raise its profile. A companion Archive report concluded that America came fairly close to using tactical nuclear weapons in 1958. The evidence here is the title alone. The page's point is the parallel: an old island crisis, read again under new pressure.
govdocs-nsarchive-News_foia_Government_a: After lawsuits and public pressure over its records practices, the government agreed to preserve White House records, and a National Security Archive briefing book page carries that agreement under a short headline. Such agreements bind an administration to keep the papers, messages, and call records the Presidential Records Act covers, so release can be fought over later with the evidence intact. Only the page capture survives here. It marks a checkpoint in the contest over whether a president's record belongs to the president or the public.
hanshu-ban-gu-chinese:
Ban Gu, a court scholar of the Eastern Han, wrote the Hanshu, the Book of Han, in the first century CE. It tells the story of the Western Han house, from its founding to the fall of Wang Mang. The text here is the full work in its original classical Chinese, drawn from Chinese Wikisource.

Annals of the emperors come first, then tables, then treatises on rites, law, food and goods, rivers, and the heavens. Biographies of ministers, rebels, scholars, and envoys fill the rest. The Hanshu set the form that all later Chinese dynastic histories would follow. It stays the base source for two centuries of China.
heartbreak-house:
George Bernard Shaw wrote Heartbreak House between 1913 and 1916, calling it a fantasia in the Russian manner on English themes. His long preface names the target: cultured, leisured Europe before the First World War. Shaw compares his house to the country homes in Chekhov and Tolstoy. Nice people read, talk, and do nothing while disaster loads its guns outside.

Young Ellie Dunn arrives at Captain Shotover's Sussex house, invited by his daughter Hesione Hushabye. The old captain pursues concentration and invents explosives between naps. A burglar, a romantic lady, and Ellie's broken engagement stir the weekend. Talk of money, love, and war circles without resolution. Shaw lets charm and futility share every scene. Readers get his darkest drawing-room comedy, where an idle class drifts toward a reckoning it cannot imagine.
hilda-wade-a-woman-with-tenacity-of-purp:
Grant Allen's Hilda Wade, published in 1899, was his last work, and its publishers' note tells a famous story. Allen died with the final chapter only roughly sketched. His friend and neighbour Arthur Conan Doyle discussed the plan with him, absorbed what Allen intended, and wrote the ending himself. The note calls it a beautiful and pathetic act of friendship.

Hilda Wade is a nurse at St. Nathaniel's Hospital with an uncanny gift of intuition. She serves Professor Sebastian, the great physiologist who preaches the gospel of germs. Episode by episode she reads patients, poisons, and impostors at a glance. Her tenacity of purpose aims at one hidden enemy through all the cases. The narrator, a young doctor, watches her gift with awe. Doyle's borrowed pen closes a series that joined detection to medical science.
houhanshu-fan-ye-chinese:
Fan Ye compiled the Hou Hanshu, the Book of the Later Han, in the fifth century CE, and he died before he could add its treatises. His history covers the Eastern Han house, from its restoration in 25 CE to its fall in 220. The text here is the complete work in classical Chinese, from Chinese Wikisource.

Imperial annals lead, followed by long runs of biography: empresses, princes, ministers, scholars, generals, and men of strange arts. Fan Ye wrote with a sharp, judgmental pen. His book is the standard source for the last two centuries of Han rule. Every later study of the age builds on it.
in-freedom-s-cause: In Freedom's Cause, G. A. Henty's Wallace and Bruce tale. Scottish freedom. This book preserves that historical novel. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact.
inspector-french-s-greatest-case: Inspector French's Greatest Case, Freeman Wills Crofts's detective novel. The inspector's triumph. This book preserves that mystery. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it.
laperouse:
Ernest Scott wrote this life of the French explorer Laperouse. A monument to Laperouse overlooks Botany Bay in Sydney, Scott notes. Many visitors see it yet know little of the man.

Chapters cover Laperouse's youth, his naval career, and his love story. The great voyage of exploration fills the middle of the book. His ships reached Botany Bay, then vanished into mystery. Captain Dillon's later discovery helped solve that loss. Scott tells a sea story that ends in one of exploration's famous puzzles. Scott writes for general readers, not naval specialists. The Botany Bay ending gives Australians a special stake in the tale.
mary-louise:
Mary Louise opens a set of books sold as the Bluebird Books. The title page names Edith Van Dyne as the author. A note from the sellers speaks straight to young readers.

They say Mary Louise is a real, human girl, much like the reader. The first heads promise an argument, Gran'pa Jim, and a surprise. Then sands shift, and a formal probe puts the girl under a cloud. The sellers praise tales that are wholesome yet full of action. Later heads name Irene, a letter from home, and a confession. School life and family strain mix in this first Bluebird tale.
melbourne-house:
Susan Warner wrote Melbourne House under the name Elizabeth Wetherell. She had won fame as the author of The Wide, Wide World. Ward Lock issued this London copy in 1907, from the 1864 book.

A verse from Proverbs heads the title page, on a child's deeds. Daisy leads the tale, and her question opens chapter one. A pony chaise, a birthday, a ham, and strawberries follow in order. Trout, a field of battle, and a wounded hand come later in the heads. Daisy grows through small trials at home and at school. Each short head marks one step in her young moral life.
miscellaneous-prose:
George Meredith's shorter prose opens with his introduction to Thackeray's The Four Georges. Meredith traces Thackeray from his birth in Calcutta in 1811. He follows him through Charterhouse school and then Cambridge. He praises Thackeray's quiet eye, his humour, and his gift for sharp, funny criticism.

The parodies, Meredith argues, judge their targets better than grave reviews do. This volume also holds A Pause in the Strife and Concession to the Celt. A memoir of Leslie Stephen follows. Meredith's letters to the Morning Post, sent from the war in Italy, close the book. They show the famed novelist at work as critic and poet too.
model-speeches-for-practise:
Grenville Kleiser published this practice collection with Funk and Wagnalls in 1920. Kleiser had taught public speaking at Yale Divinity School. His earlier books include How to Speak in Public and Great Speeches and How to Make Them. The volume opens with his own introduction on the aims and purposes of speaking.

Model speeches by famous voices follow for students to study and rehearse. James Russell Lowell contributes a piece on after-dinner speaking. Ralph Waldo Emerson's England, Mother of Nations comes next in the contents. Kleiser's premise is that speakers learn by practicing proven models, the way musicians practice scales, before facing an audience themselves.
mohammed-ali-and-his-house: Luise Mühlbach wrote this historical novel about Mohammed Ali and his house in Egypt, and Chapman Coleman translated it from the German. Mühlbach was a prolific German novelist of historical romances. The hosted sample, however, preserves no readable content from the novel itself. It contains only the Project Gutenberg header, naming the author and translator. Readers therefore get the book's identity and subject, Egypt's famous ruler and court, but the sample offers none of its scenes or dialogue.
monsieur-du-miroir-from-mosses-from-an-o:
Nathaniel Hawthorne studies a mysterious gentleman in this sketch from Mosses from an Old Manse. Monsieur du Miroir is, the narrator says, the acquaintance he has studied most and knows least. The two share a permanent joint interest, though the narrator never chose it. Monsieur bears an indisputable personal resemblance to him.

The gentleman never speaks, though his lips move and his face shifts with expression. He wears mourning at family funerals, and some trace his line to Spanish knights of the mirror. Hawthorne's joke is philosophical: the monsieur is his own reflection, the self a man watches daily. The sketch turns a mirror into a parable of self-knowledge.
more-nonsense:
Edward Lear fills this sequel to his nonsense books with pictures, rhymes, and botany. The contents promise Nonsense Botany first. Then come one hundred nonsense pictures and rhymes, and twenty-six more rhymes and pictures. Lear invents plants with names like Barkia Howlaloudia and Enkoopia Chickabiddia.

His botany plate names continue: Shoebootia Utilis, Washtubbia Circularis, and Tigerlillia Terribilis. Each plant is drawn as if for a serious scientific work, which is the joke. Lear, the artist who taught Queen Victoria drawing, made nonsense a form of art. Children and adults still quote his limericks and copy his absurd gardens.
more-translations-from-the-chinese:
Arthur Waley published this second volume of Chinese translations with Alfred A. Knopf in 1919. It follows his Hundred and Seventy Chinese Poems. The contents open with Ch'ü Yüan's Great Summons, an ancient shamanistic poem. A prose letter by Wang Wei follows.

Li Po, the great Tang poet, dominates the next pages. Waley translates Drinking Alone by Moonlight and Waking from Drunkenness on a Spring Day. His plain, musical versions introduced Chinese poetry to English readers who knew none of the language. This volume deepened that introduction, moving from Tang lyrics back to the oldest Chinese verse.
mother-goose-in-prose:
L. Frank Baum turned the Mother Goose rhymes into prose stories in this 1901 volume. Maxfield Parrish illustrated it with some of his most famous pictures. Each chapter tells the story behind a rhyme. Sing a Song of Sixpence comes first, then the story of Little Boy Blue.

The Cat and the Fiddle, the Black Sheep, and Old King Cole follow. Mistress Mary, Jack Horner, and the Man in the Moon get their tales too. Baum wrote the book before The Wonderful Wizard of Oz made him famous. His expansions give the rhyme figures families, motives, and small adventures for children who ask why.
my-strangest-case:
Guy Boothby's mystery novel first came out in 1901. Boothby had won fame with Dr. Nikola and Pharos the Egyptian. The tale runs in four parts, told by its narrator. A contents list was added for this HTML edition.

Catalog copy says a detective is hired to hunt two men. The pair fled with treasure found in Burma's jungles. Boothby writes in a brisk, bold style of empire adventure. Dark holes, revolvers, and falls fill the picture captions. Miss Kitwater greets Mr. Fairfax in one tense scene. The case mixes crime, travel, and greed in the author's best sensational manner.
nasa-tm-19650003083-dynamic-response-of-:
David N Bowditch and Fred A Wilcox at Lewis Research Center studied how a supersonic diffuser responds when parts of it are made to oscillate. A diffuser slows fast air inside an engine inlet. Here the moving parts were the spike and the bypass, tested one at a time.

The pair measured the size and timing shift of static pressure changes inside the diffuser. Tests ran at Mach 1.8 and Mach 2.0, with a J53 engine and three cold-pipe setups of different length. The data show how inlet pressure behaves when conditions will not sit still.
nasa-tm-19670014642-computing-the-pseudo:
Christopher R. Herron, of NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland, wrote this computing paper in November 1966. It explains how to compute the pseudo-inverse of a matrix. The pseudo-inverse stands in for an ordinary inverse when a system of equations has none. It gives engineers and scientists a standard way to handle such problems.

Herron describes an orthogonalization algorithm that produces the pseudo-inverse, then gives a complete FORTRAN program that carries the algorithm out. The opening sections define the concept through the conditions first set down by Penrose, who called it the generalized inverse. The paper keeps to real matrices for simplicity, while noting that most results also hold for complex ones. Acknowledgments credit E. R. Lancaster for supervision and theoretical help, and G. H. Wyatt for programming skill during debugging.
nasa-tm-19670026333-modification-of-the-:
NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland issued this preliminary engineering report on changes to its Optical Research Facility. The catalog record says the building modifications were made for satellite tracking with lasers. Laser tracking was then a young technique that needed purpose-fitted space, stable mountings, and carefully planned building services.

The surviving contents pages detail the services side of the project. Work covers an addition to the existing building and a separate field elevated laboratory. Plumbing sections address water, sanitary, and storm systems, plus fire protection for the field laboratory. Heating, ventilation, and air conditioning are specified for both structures. Electrical sections estimate loads and lay out power distribution, lighting, utility power, and grounding. Together they show the practical building work behind an optical tracking station.
nasa-tm-19680004519-designs-of-experimen:
Arthur G. Holms, at the Lewis Research Center in Cleveland, presented this paper at an Army design of experiments conference in Virginia in November 1967. He treats statistical designs as telescoping sequences of blocks. Each block of trials builds on the last instead of starting over.

In his sequences, the first block's results fit a simple model. Those same results are kept and combined with new blocks, fitting richer models step by step. Nothing measured is wasted. The idea grew out of optimum-seeking experiments in alloy development. NASA had used such hunts to improve engine materials for the supersonic transport.
nasa-tm-19680017367-the-salt-specificity:
L. I. Hochstein and B. P. Dalton of Ames Research Center examine a salt-dependent enzyme in this paper, presented in May 1967. The enzyme, an NADH oxidase, came from an extreme halophile, a microbe that lives in very salty settings. It works only at high solute concentrations.

Extracts of the microbe showed the enzyme accepted several salts in place of sodium chloride. Potassium, rubidium, and cesium chlorides worked with little loss of activity. Ammonium chloride worked partly, while lithium chloride failed completely. Among anions, chloride had no unique hold either. Bromide, nitrate, and iodide were essentially ineffective, while acetate, formate, citrate, and sulfate proved suitable substitutes.
nasa-tm-19690028502-development-of-space:
C. N. Irvine, of the Manufacturing Engineering Laboratory at Marshall Space Flight Center, reports window assembly development in this July 1969 memorandum, report number 53853. The assemblies serve a space station's pressure shell. Their special feature is explosive cutting: a shaped charge can slice a clean opening through the window panel when crews need one.

Chapters cover design and fabrication before the test series begins. Tests cut twenty-centimeter holes in panels at two charge loadings, shown in photographs. Smaller fifteen-centimeter holes follow, including a vented version and a detonator standoff trial. A pressure cartridge is pictured among the hardware. Conclusions and recommendations close the development report for the prototype assemblies.
nasa-tm-19720011008-system-evaluation-fr:
J K Baumeister and E H Hopper of the Marshall Space Flight Center wrote this technical note in March 1972, as NASA TM X-2521. It solves a common problem in systems analysis. Engineers often know a system only by its sampled impulse response. That list of numbers is awkward for further design work. What they really need is the transfer function, a compact formula for the system's behavior.

The authors found a procedure based on rational approximation. It computes the transfer function from a limited number of response values. The system's order does not need to be known in advance. Moving the result into the other common domain is also easy. Short, incomplete response records can still yield a usable model.
nerves-and-common-sense:
Annie Payson Call gathered Nerves and Common Sense from pieces first printed in The Ladies' Home Journal. Call also wrote Power Through Repose and As a Matter of Course. She thanks editor Edward Bok for his helpful titles. This copy is a new and enlarged edition.

Chapters treat habit and nervous strain, and how women can keep from being nervous. Others ask why Mrs Smith gets on my nerves, and deal with trying family members and irritable husbands. Call sets quiet against chronic excitement, and rest against hurry. Her counsel is plain and household sized, aimed at daily calm rather than doctors' cures.
nitro-explosives-a-practical-treatise:
P. Gerald Sanford, a public analyst for Penzance and a trained chemist, wrote Nitro-Explosives as a practical treatise. This copy is the second edition, revised and enlarged. Sanford had worked as resident chemist at explosives works in Stowmarket and Hayle. He also advised the Cotton Powder Company.

His preface promises a brief but thorough account of nitrated substances. He covers their properties, their manufacture, and how to test them. The subtitle names fulminates, smokeless powders, and celluloid among the subjects. His account of nitro-glycerine and the gelatine dynamites, he claims, beats any like book in this country. Miners, blasters, and powder makers were his readers.
notes-on-the-apocalypse:
David Steele, pastor of the Reformed Presbyterian Congregation in Philadelphia, published his Notes on the Apocalypse there in 1870. Young and Ferguson printed the book. An appendix adds dissertations on some apocalyptic symbols. Steele also adds animadversions, or sharp remarks, on readings by learned expositors in Britain and America.

He submits the work under the auspices of the Reverend John Cunningham, a missionary to the Jews in London. Events of providence, Steele writes, are the signs of the times and the counterpart of prophecy. Prophecy and providence reflect light upon each other, he argues. Only the Wonderful Counsellor, he adds, can make either clear. The book reads Revelation with strict, old faith.
on-compromise:
John Morley wrote this famous essay on truth and compromise. Macmillan first printed this edition in 1886. A note dated May 1877 explains his modest aim. Morley says an essay should only open questions. It should indicate points, suggest cases, and sketch outlines.

The opening quote stresses putting truth in first place. Morley asks when compromise betrays truth in public life. He compares England's mood with that of other countries. He traces the decay of recent hopes and aspirations. The essay shaped Victorian debate about principle in politics. It still challenges readers who face hard moral choices.
p-s-correspondence-from-mosses-from-an-o:
Nathaniel Hawthorne's sketch P.'s Correspondence, from Mosses from an Old Manse, is built on a melancholy conceit. His unfortunate friend P. has lost the thread of his life. Intervals of disordered reason jumble past and present in his mind. Without stirring from his little whitewashed room, he is nevertheless a great traveler. He meets personages long invisible to any eye save his own.

Hawthorne doubts it is mere delusion; it is a sport of the imagination given morbid energy by disease. P., who always hankered after literary fame and failed to win it by reason's light, may have stumbled on it in his misty excursions beyond sanity. His letter, dated London, February 29, 1845, begins by wondering whether he is not still an inhabitant of that wearisome little chamber.
paz-la-fausse-maitresse:
Balzac's Paz, also called La Fausse Maitresse, opens in Paris in September 1835. Clementine du Rouvre, a great heiress of the faubourg Saint-Germain, marries Comte Adam Laginski, a young Polish exile. Her spendthrift father has squandered a fortune, but uncles and aunts settle theirs on her.

Adam's friend Captain Paz shares the household and serves it with hidden devotion, for he loves Clementine in secret. Katharine Prescott Wormeley translated the tale into English. It is a bittersweet story from the Human Comedy about loyalty, concealment, and a love that must never speak.
pen-drawing-an-illustrated-treatise: The sample hosted here shows only the front matter of Pen Drawing: An Illustrated Treatise, the title page, acknowledgements, and list of illustrations, with no instruction text visible. The title page names Charles D. Maginnis, formerly instructor in illustration at the Cowles Art School and in pen drawing at the Boston Architectural Club, in a seventh edition. The illustration list credits Joseph Pennell, Bertram G. Goodhue, Herbert Railton, and Daniel Vierge among the artists whose work the treatise uses.
podcast-joerogan-3yrKVu35uSE:
Filmmaker James Fox joins the Joe Rogan Experience for episode 2246. Fox directs documentaries on UFO cases, built from witness interviews and official records. His visits to Rogan tend to be detailed briefings rather than loose chat, and this one follows that pattern.

Fox walks through the cases and footage he has gathered, including testimony from pilots and people who claim close encounters. Rogan asks how the film work is done and which claims Fox trusts most. For listeners who follow disclosure, the episode is a compact update on the evidence Fox finds strongest and the stories still unexplained.
podcast-joerogan-GmHwG2p_esE:
Religion scholar Gary Laderman joins the Joe Rogan Experience for episode 1565, a rare academic visit for the show. Laderman studies how Americans handle the sacred and the profane, from funerals to fame. His subject is belief in a country that claims to have outgrown it.

He and Rogan talk about death rites, the cult of celebrities, and why sacred feelings keep surfacing in secular life. Laderman brings a professor's store of odd facts, and Rogan brings the layman's blunt questions. The episode is a thoughtful tour of American religion in disguise, told through funerals, fandom, and the things people treat as holy.
podcast-joerogan-JUePtc0bJSE:
Comedian and libertarian Dave Smith returns to Joe Rogan for episode 2474. Smith hosts Part of the Problem, a sharp political comedy show. He is a frequent and favored Rogan guest.

The pair range over war, power, and media lies with ease. Smith mixes jokes with a strict antiwar case. Rogan trusts his read on the news of the day. The episode is funny and pointed in equal parts. It suits listeners who want their liberty talk served by a comic who knows both the stage and the issues. Liberty and laughs share the mic in balance.
podcast-joerogan-OR7vtVnU5SE:
Joe Rogan turns to the alien skeletons shown in Mexico and the doctors who checked them in a segment from his show. The specimens were shown to Mexico's lawmakers and split the world at once. Rogan hosts the look at the case.

Rogan works through what the doctors claimed the scans showed and what other experts said in reply. He asks why such finds so often land in a blur of hype and fraud claims. The segment is short and hot with doubt on all sides. Listeners get the core of a wild tale. The library holds the file as an archive record, without a side taken.
poems-of-purpose:
Ella Wheeler Wilcox titled this 1919 London collection Poems of Purpose, and the contents announce their errands plainly: Happiness, Seeking for Happiness, the Things that Count, Limitless, Certitude, and Compassion. Gay and Hancock published the volume in Covent Garden in the year after the Great War ended. Wilcox believed a poem should do work in a reader's life, and these pieces are tools, each built to deliver one usable thought.

Love in several states runs through the list, Love itself, Three Souls, and When Love Is Lost, beside civic pieces such as America and War Mothers. A Good Sport opens the book, and Gypsying closes it, framing duty with freedom. Taken with her other themed volumes, Purpose shows the system behind Wilcox's fame: sort the feelings of ordinary life, and give each one a short, rhymed, memorable treatment.
poise:
D. Starke wrote Poise: How to Attain It, translated by Francis Medhurst and published in the Mental Efficiency Series in 1916. Its motto states the doctrine in one line: poise is a power derived from the mastery of self. Part one argues the need, naming timidity and awkwardness as enemies that have always held capable people back. That is true never more than in the demanding life of today, where first impressions decide so much.

Part two gives the method, contrasting modesty with effrontery and prescribing physical exercises in four series, plus practical drills, toward what Starke calls the supreme achievement. The book belongs to the era's self-culture shelf, beside memory training and will-power manuals, and its premise is democratic. Poise is not breeding or luck but a trainable habit of body and nerve that any reader can practice.
popular-tales-from-the-norse:
Sir George Webbe Dasent translated and introduced this famous gathering of Norwegian folk tales, collected by Asbjörnsen and Moe and Englished for the first time here. Dasent fronts the tales with a long introductory essay on the origin and diffusion of popular tales. Arguing that stories travel across nations like seeds on the wind, and a chapter on Norse mythology to arm the reader. The tales then speak for themselves, in Dasent's hearty, fireside voice.

East o' the Sun and West o' the Moon leads the beloved titles, with Why the Sea Is Salt. The Giant Who Had No Heart in His Body, the Mastermaid, the Princess on the Glass Hill, and the boy Boots, who out-eats a troll and outwits everyone. Dasent's versions fixed these stories in English childhood. Generations learned the stumpy-tailed bear and Gudbrand on the Hillside from these pages.
power-through-repose:
Annie Payson Call wrote Power Through Repose, a new edition with additions of her influential book on relaxation. Her motto, borrowed from François Delsarte, states the creed: personality binds, universality expands. A second epigraph from W. R. Alger pictures the body perfectly adjusted, perfectly supplied with force, and working with the greatest economy, fitted to be a perfect instrument of impression, experience, and expression.

Her first chapter, the Guidance of the Body, complains that shelves groan with advice on food, air, and clothing while nobody teaches the better use of the machine itself. Strain, she argues, can be studiously abandoned through training as regular as any muscle work, climbing back step by step from perverted habits to an orderly life. Call's book founded a school of American relaxation teaching; nervous readers of the 1890s treated it as medicine.
proposals-for-building-in-every-county-a:
An unnamed writer laid a plan before Parliament in a pamphlet printed in London in 1677, urging that every county build a working almshouse or hospital. The aim was twofold: to employ the poor and to grow a home trade in linen cloth.

The plan promises work and keep for poor people and children from age five or six, an end to begging, and relief for parishes crushed by poor rates. It also promises to keep at home the large sums then spent abroad on linen. Readers get an early scheme of workhouse reform.
punky-dunk-and-the-mouse:
Punky Dunk and the Mouse is a picture book in rhyme for small children, issued by P. F. Volland and Company of Chicago under a 1912 copyright. Like its companions in the series, it names no author, and its title page leaves a blank line for the name of the child it was made for.

The sly kitten spends a morning in the cellar hunting a fat little mouse. He sits by the mouse's hole near the coal, beside a trap baited with cheese, and pretends to nap while he watches for the gleam of two bright eyes. Soon the mouse creeps out and runs about, and Punky smiles to himself.
raabe-die-chronik-der-sperlingsgasse:
An old man looks back over the life of one Berlin street in Raabe's first novel, Die Chronik der Sperlingsgasse, given here in German. The Chronicle of Sparrow Lane gathers neighbors, loves, and losses into a single remembered neighborhood. Raabe published the book at twenty-five, and it announced a major talent.

Warm, nostalgic, and beautifully observed, the novel made readers call its author the German Dickens, a name that stuck. Each household on the lane opens like a small world with its own weather. Joy and grief share doorsteps in his telling. The book remains the friendliest doorway into Raabe's long career. Its lane still feels inhabited, door by door.
red-pepper-s-patients-with-an-account-of:
Grace S. Richmond returned to her doctor hero in this 1918 book from Doubleday, Page, printed at Garden City, New York. Its full title singles out one case: Anne Linton's, in particular. A front picture shows Red Pepper Burns, M.D., at work among those he treats.

Chapters open with an intelligent prescription and a place called Little Hungary, then turn to Anne Linton's temperature. Two red heads, heavy local mails, white lilacs, and expert diagnosis fill the middle list. One chapter is named The Surgical Firing Line, and another The Truth About Susquehanna. The cases mix town practice with strain, love, and risk.
sanguozhi-chen-shou-chinese:
Chen Shou, an official of the Jin court, wrote the Sanguozhi, the Records of the Three Kingdoms, around 289 CE. After the Han fell, China split into Wei, Shu, and Wu, and Chen Shou gave each state its own book. The text here is the full work in classical Chinese, from Chinese Wikisource.

The records are built from biographies: founders, generals, ministers, and queens, each life packed with deeds and judgments. Chen Shou wrote close to the events, from court files and fresh memory. His book is the base source for the Three Kingdoms age. The famous novel of that age grew from these dry, sharp lives.
scotus-ordinatio-opus-oxoniense:
Scotus's Ordinatio, long known as the Oxford Work, appears here in the 1891 Vives printing of his collected works. The Ordinatio is his great commentary on the Sentences of Peter Lombard, the set text of medieval theology. Scotus lectured on the Sentences at Oxford, and the work grew into his summa, left unfinished at his death in 1308.

Across its books, the commentary treats God, creation, the Incarnation, and the sacraments with unmatched subtlety. Scotus defends the freedom of the will and the special privilege of Mary, doctrines that marked his school for centuries. The text is dense because the questions were hard and the standards exact. The Vives edition, reprinting Wadding's older collection, was the standard nineteenth-century way to read the Subtle Doctor's whole theology in one vast work.
seven-maids-of-far-cathay-being-english-:
Bing Ding compiled these English notes from a Chinese class book, with pictures by Ai Lang. Seven girls in the graduating class of the Woman's Anglo-Chinese College at Neuchang wrote the notes as a game across their last six months. A stenographer took the pieces down as the girls read them aloud.

College leaders arranged the notes and printed them just as first produced, with no revision. Sections bear plain role names: Biographer, Correspondent, Diarist, Essayist, Folklorist, and Genius. Western readers meet Chinese students' fresh English voices, full of humor and pride in their college life.
sex-and-common-sense:
A. Maude Royden, assistant preacher at the City Temple in London from 1918 to 1920, wrote this plain talk on relations between the sexes. Royden opens by calling the sex problem a noble one, fit for open thought rather than whispers and jokes. She insists that most readers care about normal life, not vice.

Royden argues that the sex instinct ranks among the great powers of human nature, and that its misuse brings shame and pain. She asks how plain men and women can live on a higher, finer pattern. Her aim is growth: rightly, gladly, and humanely ordered love.
shiji-sima-qian-chinese:
Sima Qian, the grand historian of the Han court, finished the Shiji, the Records of the Grand Historian, around 91 BCE. His father began the work, and Sima Qian gave it its final shape after shame and prison. The text here is the complete work in classical Chinese, from Chinese Wikisource.

One hundred thirty chapters mix basic annals, tables, treatises on rites and the heavens, the tales of great houses, and lives of single men. The reach runs from the Yellow Emperor to the reigning Han house. The Shiji founded the way China writes its past. Its biographies still set the model for Chinese prose.
sketches-from-memory-from-mosses-from-an:
Nathaniel Hawthorne wrote these sketches from memory for his Mosses from an Old Manse. The Notch of the White Mountains opens the set. In mid-September the party rides up the Saco valley from Bartlett, between mountain walls, along a road as level at times as a church aisle.

Height rises on height until clouds hang below the peaks. Red slide paths scar the slopes where earth, stones, and trees once thundered down. Settlers once feared northern Indians sweeping through these defiles, Hawthorne recalls. His prose turns a stage ride into awe at old, bright, perilous hills.
songs-and-other-verse:
Songs and Other Verse forms Volume IX of the Works of Eugene Field. The volume holds his writings in prose and verse. Its opening pages print a comic letter. Field signs it with a Latin-styled name, Eugenio Agro. He writes to his brother with mock pomp. He invites a bishop and his staff to a reading. Field will read his things before a senior class. The class sits at the Chicago University. Robes and a march in at eight are part of the joke.

A note then tells of a lady's trip Southwest. She won two choice gifts there for Field. For his library she got an odd Indian blanket. It shows in sketches of his loved workshop. For Field himself she got a necktie. A diamond-back rattlesnake gave its skin for it.
songs-before-sunrise: Algernon Charles Swinburne wrote Songs Before Sunrise, first published by Ellis in 1871. The 1917 William Heinemann issue at London lists many later printings by Chatto through 1915, a Florence Press edition of 1909, and a place in the Collected Poems. Swinburne gives the book to Joseph Mazzini. His dedication tells Mazzini to take the poems, since he bade them bear his name, as fruit of the seed of his sowing, be it blossom, berry, or weed.
sonnets-and-verse:
H. Belloc gives Sonnets and Verse to John Swinnerton Phillimore. A dedication poem opens the gift. It looks back to the days of boyhood. When you and I were little tiny boys, he writes. We took a bold delight in foolish toys. Painted and misshapen, mothers brought them at night. Duckworth and Co. printed the London book. Turnbull and Spears of Edinburgh made it.

Belloc asks his friend to take the flawed toys. Phillimore keeps the child's keener part, he says. In his heart the toys may gain a perfect form. The gift rests on the content a known love brings. Set at the head of sonnets and verse, the poem frames the set. Youth's toys go to an old friend. Love, the poem hopes, will mend their shape.
sonnets-from-the-portuguese: Elizabeth Barrett Browning wrote Sonnets from the Portuguese, printed by the Caradoc Press at Bedford Park, Chiswick, London, in MDCCCCVI, that is, 1906. The opening pages give an index of first lines in place of the poems' text. It begins: I thought once how Theocritus had sung; But only three in all God's universe; Unlike are we, unlike, O princely Heart; and Thou hast thy calling to some palace-floor. Go from me and If thou must love me stand in the list.
stray-pearls-memoirs-of-margaret-de-riba:
Stray Pearls: Memoirs of Margaret de Ribaumont, Viscountess of Bellaise, by Charlotte M. Yonge, dated 1883 in this printing, tells a French family's story across the wars of the Fronde. Its chapter heads move between the English and French courts of the seventeenth century.

The contents begin at Whitehall before the cobwebs, pass through a little mutual aversion, Celadon and Chloe, and the Salon Bleu, then reach life in garrison and a victory dearly bought. Widow and wife, Marguerite to the rescue, the firebrand of the Bocage, the two queens, cavaliers in exile, and the barricades follow. Yonge mixes court intrigue with family duty and faith.
studies-in-the-psychology-of-sex-volume-:
Volume III of Havelock Ellis's Studies in the Psychology of Sex, dated 1927, holds Analysis of the Sexual Impulse, Love and Pain, and The Sexual Impulse in Women. A preface to the second edition reports the volume fully revised and enlarged, with new case histories added in an appendix.

Ellis says the main doctrines of ten years before still stand. Yet new work on hormones had reshaped knowledge in the field. Those hormones are the internal secretions of the ductless glands. They bear on how the sexual instinct is produced in the body. His own account ties the impulse to a physical process of building and release, while claiming it can stand apart from unsettled questions of ultimate origin.
sunrise:
William Black, author of Shandon Bells and Strange Adventures of a Phaeton, published the novel Sunrise at New York through John B. Alden in 1883. Its chapter titles promise travel and intrigue: a first interview, pleadings, a house in Curzon Street, pioneers, and a night in Venice.

Later chapters bring a Russian episode, a man named Calabressa, an evening at the Culturverein, a performance of Fidelio, and a father and daughter at odds. Black sets private feeling against secret societies and foreign politics, moving his people from London drawing rooms to Italy and beyond. The chapter heads, from Jacta Est Alea, the die is cast, onward, mark a story of vows, evasions, and a talisman.
susan-lenox-her-fall-and-rise:
David Graham Phillips's Susan Lenox: Her Fall and Rise appears here in Volume I of the D. Appleton edition of 1917, printed at New York and London with a portrait of the author. A tribute at the front mourns Phillips himself, written by a friend who still looks for his tall, boyish figure on Fifth Avenue.

The tribute calls Phillips the most honest man its writer ever knew. His clear blue eyes scorned untruth. His knightly mind hoisted the burdens of the world. It set them onto young shoulders, his own. The novel behind that praise follows its title's hard arc: a country girl's fall into the city's underworld and her long climb back, told with Phillips's usual anger at sham and corruption.
the-after-house:
Mary Roberts Rinehart wrote The After House. It is a mystery novel in twenty-five chapters, told in the first person. Chapter heads promise a painted ship and a terrible night. A found axe, prisoners, and mutiny talk come next. Tales from the stewardess, the first mate, and Oleson fill the late heads.

Chapter one, I Plan a Voyage, tells how the narrator was funded. A bequest from an elder brother paid his way. It saw him through a small Ohio college. It paid for four years at a medical school in the East. He says he hardly knows why he chose medicine. A bent for the surgeon's bold trade may explain it. A family line of doctors may explain it too. Readers board a yacht where wealth, drink, and an axe murder trap a small crew at sea.
the-angel-in-the-house:
Coventry Patmore's long poem on wedded love appears here in Cassell's National Library, printed at London in 1891. Patmore inscribes the poem to the memory of her by whom and for whom, he says, he became a poet. An introduction tells how the work first came out in two parts, in 1854 and 1856.

The editor notes that Patmore later reworked the poem with great care. It has since won, the note claims, a lasting place among the home books of the English people. Cheap wide spread, Patmore felt, would not hurt a finer library edition. The best use of writing, he held, is the spread of verse given to the sacred love of home.
the-ballad-of-the-white-horse:
G. K. Chesterton warns readers in a prefatory note that his ballad does not claim to be history. Alfred is a real king, he argues, but the legends about him are the most important thing. Chesterton deals with Alfred as a popular legend still alive in England.

Three tales show his method. One links Alfred's final victory to the Vale of the White Horse in Berkshire. Others tell of Alfred playing the harp in the Danish camp, and of Alfred with a woman and her cakes. Chesterton picks each tale because people told it, not because records prove it. The poem follows old ballad makers, who wrote from hearsay and tradition.
the-book-of-nonsense:
Edward Lear made the Book of Nonsense, a set of short comic verses with his own drawings. He gave the book to the great-grandchildren, grand-nephews, and grand-nieces of Edward, 13th Earl of Derby. Most of the verses and art were first made for their parents. A short verse at the front tells of an Old Derry down Derry who made a book to make small folk shake with glee.

Each verse takes one odd soul and spins a small joke in five lines. An old man finds that two owls, a hen, four larks, and a wren have built nests in his beard. A young lady of Ryde buys clogs and small spotty dogs and walks about Ryde. An old man with a long nose snaps that those who think it too long are wrong.
the-butterfly-house:
Mary E. Wilkins Freeman wrote The Butterfly House, put out in New York by Dodd, Mead and Company in 1912, with illustrations by Paul Julien Meylan. Freeman had also written A Humble Romance and A New England Nun. Chapter I is spent on its setting: Fairbridge, a little New Jersey village, or rather city. It had won municipal government some years before, over the protest of far-seeing citizens.

Fairbridge, the tale says, was a misnomer. A first-time visitor, driven round its rural streets, would ask: why Fairbridge? Bridges there were none, save those the trains thundered over to and from New York. Nor could an unbiased eye call the place fair. Worse than the name was the spirit: Fairbridge was tragically petty, since it saw itself great, and narrowness there did not reign but tyrannised.
the-cab-of-the-sleeping-horse: John Reed Scott wrote The Cab of the Sleeping Horse, put out in New York by the A. L. Burt Company in 1916, by arrangement with G. P. Putnam's Sons. William van Dresser drew the front plate. Scott had also written The Woman in Question and The Man in Evening Clothes. The chapters start with The Photograph, The Voice on the Wire, and Visitors. Surprises, The Story, Decoyed, and Skirmishing lead to Half a Lie. Carpenter, The Marquis, and The Slip of Paper close the heads shown.
the-canadian-photoplay-title-of-the-land:
The Canadian is the photoplay title of The Land of Promise, a novelization by D. Torbett of W. Somerset Maugham's play, made into a Paramount Picture starring Thomas Meighan. Grosset and Dunlap published it, under a copyright of 1914 held by Edward J. Clode, and a plate caption promises the moment when love for her husband is finally born in Nora.

Chapter I opens on Nora waking to a sense of well-being, her youth reasserting itself after whatever strain came before. The book is a film tie-in of its era: a stage play turned stage story turned screen vehicle, carrying its heroine's slow change of heart as the advertised heart of the plot.
the-christmas-banquet-from-mosses-from-a:
Nathaniel Hawthorne wrote this tale, drawn from his unpublished Allegories of the Heart and framed by talk in a summer house. Roderick unfolds a few sheets of manuscript for Rosina and the sculptor. His former sad experience, he says, has given him insight into the gloomy mysteries of the human heart.

Roderick compares that wandering to being lost in a dark cavern with a torch fast dying. Yet one figure still puzzles him past solving. The man looks like a man, perhaps a better specimen than most, and seems wise, refined, and outwardly moral.
