The sculptor could carve his shape in marble, and some future science might lend him a fine mockery of mind. Still, Roderick argues, the last touch of a divine Creator is lacking. What the spirit demands from another spirit, this figure cannot give.
the-circular-staircase:
Mary Roberts Rinehart built this mystery around a country house and its staircase, told by the woman who rented the house. The contents run to thirty-four chapters, with titles that name a link cuff-button, a sprained ankle, a hole in the wall, and a ladder out of place. Names recur through the list: Halsey, Gertrude, Louise, and Thomas.

Chapter I opens the narrator's own account in her voice. She calls it the story of how a middle-aged spinster lost her mind, deserted her city home, and took a furnished house for the summer. That dry self-mockery sets the tone for the puzzles that follow. A bank, a disappearance, a tramp with toothache, and Anne Watson's story all enter the contents. Rinehart mixes household comedy with steady dread, and the house itself, its corridors, stairs, and fireplaces, becomes the center of the case.
the-complete-book-of-cheese: Bob Brown wrote this cheese book, published in New York by the Gramercy Publishing Company in 1955, with illustrations by Eric Blegvad. Only the title page and a list of Brown's other food books are present here. The list names The Wine Cook Book and The South American Cook Book. It names many more besides, plus books written with the Browns as co-authors.Front matter alone is a thin basis, and it is all there is.
the-country-house: John Galsworthy's The Country House, dated 1907, is shown here only through its contents. Part I lists ten numbered chapters and Part II begins a fresh run of numbered chapters, reaching at least VII in what is present. No chapter titles are given, and the novel's own pages do not appear here.
the-dark-house:
I. A. R. Wylie, author of The Daughter of Brahma and The Shining Heights, published The Dark House in 1922. Part I opens on a large cigar and a small boy: at the moment Robert Stonehouse leans out of an upstairs bedroom window for fresh air, he turns eight years old.

Robert recalls a fifth birthday when he danced on his mother's bed shouting his age. He received a toy fort garrisoned with Highland soldiers from his father, and ruled a party of children he disliked. Soon after, his mother disappeared; they said she was dead. He picked flowers from other graves at Kensal Green to send her, never missed her, and hated Christine, who tried to take her place. Later his mother returned by a secret path as a creature of dreams, tall and beautiful, whom he refuses to believe is dead.
the-divine-comedy-volume-3-paradise:
Paradise closes Charles Eliot Norton's three-volume prose Divine Comedy. Its contents list traces the climb sphere by sphere. The Moon holds broken vows. Mercury holds Justinian's tale of the Roman eagle. Venus holds famed lovers. The Sun holds Thomas Aquinas and the wise. Each canto is summed up in a few plain lines before the text.

Higher spheres hold warriors of the faith, just rulers, and monks at prayer. Dante is quizzed on faith, hope, and love. The summaries give first-time readers a firm map of the poem's most abstract and bright realm.
the-dog-s-book-of-verse: J. Earl Clauson gathered The Dog's Book of Verse, printed in Boston with a 1916 copyright. A short verse at the front gives a dog's boast: never barking out of season, never biting without cause. The book is set in memory of Jack, an Airedale. Its first part is named Puppyhood, and a contents list sorts poems by theme. Only the front matter and that list are present here.
the-elene-of-cynewulf-translated-into-en:
Lucius Hudson Holt rendered The Elene of Cynewulf into English prose for Yale Studies in English, printed by Henry Holt in 1904. The poem opens with a count of years: two hundred and thirty-three winters since Christ's birth, in the sixth year of Constantine's reign over the Romans. Constantine stands as a shield to his folk, raised up by God with might.

Elene, the emperor's mother, sails to find the true cross. Cynewulf, an Anglo-Saxon poet, signed this tale of vision, battle, and a buried cross brought to light. Holt's prose keeps the old verse's grave pace.
the-four-horsemen-of-the-apocalypse:
Vicente Blasco Ibanez wrote The Four Horsemen of the Apocalypse as a novel of the Great War, turned into English by Charlotte Brewster Jordan. Three parts trace the Desnoyers family from Argentina to France.

The contents name Madariaga, the centaur, a rich ranch lord, and his kin split between France and Germany. Part two turns to the retreat, the invasion, and the banner of the Red Cross. Part three ends after the Marne, among burial fields. Ibanez sets one family's split loves against the four riders of war, pestilence, famine, and death let loose on Europe.
the-ghost-of-guir-house:
Charles Willing Beale wrote The Ghost of Guir House as a tale of mystery, printed in 1897. A mis-sent letter opens the tale on a dark night in New York.

Mr. Henley comes home to his small house in Twentieth Street to find a letter that has chased its man through crossed-out addresses. One note on it reads: Dead. Try Paul. The letter, dated from Guir House in September 1893, tells its reader he is the man long sought, though the two have never met. Beale draws Henley by slow steps into a haunted house, a lost will, and a love bound up with both.
the-girl-aviators-sky-cruise: Margaret Burnham wrote The Girl Aviators' Sky Cruise. Hurst and Company printed it in New York in 1911. Only front matter is present here. It gives the title page and a contents list of twenty-four chapters. The heads promise flight and plot. They name a new venture at Sandy Beach, a naval visitor, and a storm aloft. They name Peggy as heroine, lost drawings, and the flight of the Silver Cobweb. They also name an aerial post office, a marked bill, and a final gathering of the man-birds.
the-golden-house:
Charles Dudley Warner wrote The Golden House. Chapter I opens near midnight in a famous city studio. A picked crowd of a hundred guests has come. They will see a veil lifted from an Oriental and ancient art. The late hour gives the night a feel of moral risk. The risk feels bravely run.

Warner lists the guests with sly care. Scholars of Greek beauty came from Boston. Fair women came from Washington. Stars of official and diplomatic life came too. Most guests are from the city itself. The scene mocks a rich set. That set treats a hint of scandal as high culture. It sets the tone for a novel of wealth and show, where a golden house hides thin morals.
the-green-mouse: Robert W. Chambers wrote The Green Mouse. Edmund Frederick made the pictures in color. The book is dated 1910. It is dedicated to the author's friend John Corbin. Only front matter is present here. It gives the title page, the dedication verses, and the start of a contents list. The first heads are An Idyl of the Idle and The Idler. The third head is The Green Mouse. No chapter text is present.
the-grey-brethren-and-other-fragments-in: Michael Fairless wrote The Grey Brethren and Other Fragments in Prose and Verse. Duckworth and Company published the book in London in 1911. This is the third impression. Only front matter is present here. It gives the title page and a prefatory note. The note asks indulgence for the little book. Its true unity lies deeper, the note says. It lies in the personal gift, the communication of heart to heart. Most of its pieces appeared before, in The Pilot.
the-hall-of-fantasy-from-mosses-from-an-:
Nathaniel Hawthorne wrote The Hall of Fantasy, a sketch taken from Mosses from an Old Manse. The narrator describes a vast hall with a white marble floor, a high dome, and long rows of pillars in mixed styles. Light falls through stained and pictured glass, so the room feels like a dream that a stamp of the foot might break.

A friend inside explains the place in plain terms. The hall holds for the world of fancy the same place that an exchange holds for trade. All who have business with dreams may meet there and talk it over. Upper rooms are said to reach toward the moon, while cells below lead down to darker regions.
the-happy-days-of-the-empress-marie-loui: Imbert de Saint-Amand wrote The Happy Days of the Empress Marie Louise. Thomas Sergeant Perry translated the book. The contents trace a life in order. Early chapters cover her first years and the year 1809. Later chapters cover the wedding talks and the betrothal. The story goes on to the wedding at Vienna. It ends with the entrance into Paris and the religious ceremony. Front matter is all that is present here. The chapters themselves do not appear.
the-hero-of-hill-house: Mabel Hale wrote The Hero of Hill House. The contents list chapters about a boy named Austin. Early titles include Home and Mother and The Stricken Home. Later titles include Austin and His Father. The list goes on to The Runaway and Wayside Friends. Still later titles include The Revival and The Battle of Two Wills. The last title shown is Like the Troubled Sea. What is present here stops with the front matter. The story itself does not appear.
the-inner-house:
Walter Besant wrote this novel. Harper and Brothers published it in New York in 1888. His other books include All Sorts and Conditions of Men. The prologue is set at the Royal Institution. A visiting professor will announce a great discovery there. The theatre is crammed for his lecture. The director rushes to greet him. The physicist confides his timeline. Conviction came five years earlier. Proof came only in the last six months.

For half a year, rumors had flown from his laboratory. The place was Ganzweltweisst am Rhein. Guesses filled the papers of two continents. Some said he had learned to make food from chemicals. Others said he could send matter through space at once. Others feared a weapon that could shatter armies. Besant frames his tale with that comedy of guessing. The discovery itself would change how men live together.
the-intelligence-office-from-mosses-from:
Nathaniel Hawthorne's sketch opens in a metropolitan office. A grave figure sits at a desk in the corner. Mysterious spectacles rest on his nose. A pen sits behind his ear. He pores over a folio of ledger size. The walls carry advertisements of every kind. Articles lost, wanted, or for sale cover them. He looks like the spirit of a record. His own great volume seems made visible in him.

Customers stream in from the busy street. A mechanic seeks a cheap tenement. An Irish girl wanders from kitchen to kitchen. Her heart still hangs in her native cottage smoke. A faded beauty asks for her lost bloom. Peter Schlemihl asks for his lost shadow. An author seeks his vanished reputation. Then a misfit enters, hat awry and eyes astray. He announces that this must be the Central Intelligence Office.
the-judgment-house: Gilbert Parker wrote this South Africa novel, its contents running to thirty-nine chapters. Only the title page and contents are present here. The story does not appear. The headings mix the personal and the political. The jasmine flower and a daughter of Tyre open them. The partners meet, and a woman tells her story. The power-house and three years later follow. An arrow finds a breast midway. Wales appears, where Jigger plays his part. The Baas comes, a fiery furnace burns, and a battle cry closes the list.
the-lay-of-marie-and-vignettes-in-verse:
Matilda Betham published her poem The Lay of Marie in 1816, and a later Garland reprint joins it with her 1818 Vignettes in Verse. Donald H. Reiman supplies an introduction for that reprint. The poem opens with a long dedication in verse to Lady Bedingfeld.

Betham asks who else should receive a theme of minstrel lore drawn from earlier times. She praises her friend love of heroes and fair dames kept alive by romance and song. The dedication blends friendship, admiration, and esteem in formal couplets before the lay itself begins on medieval material.
the-leavenworth-case: Anna Katharine Green subtitled her detective novel a lawyer story. Only the title page and the start of the contents are present here. Book one chapters cover a great case and a coroner inquest. Facts and deductions, a clue, expert testimony, and Mary Leavenworth follow in the list. Book two, headed Henry Clavering, begins in the list as well. The investigation of the Leavenworth murder, and detective Gryce work in later chapters, does not appear in this record beyond those titles.
the-lerouge-case: Emile Gaboriau wrote his French detective novel, first published in 1863 according to the record heading. Only the title page and a bare contents list of nineteen numbered chapters are present here, with no chapter titles and no story text at all. The murder inquiry that made Gaboriau famous, and his detective Lecoq, cannot be seen in this record beyond the book name and its author.
the-life-and-perambulations-of-a-mouse:
Dorothy Kilner wrote her children tale in 1783 and 1784, and an introduction sets the storytelling scene. A severe winter snow confines a large party at Meadow Hall, where young folk and elders share the shelter. Mornings go to reading, and the rest of the day to dancing, singing, and games.

When known stories run out, a sprightly girl proposes that each person tell the history of their own life. A mouse narrator fits that game in the tale proper. Kilner uses an animal voice to teach children manners, kindness, and care in daily conduct.
the-lighthouse: R. M. Ballantyne, author of The Coral Island, wrote his tale of the Bell Rock lighthouse for young readers. Only the title page and a detailed contents list are present here. Twenty-nine chapters cover a press gang, a burglary, and storms on the Pharos. Life in the beacon, smugglers dosed with gin, and the lighthouse completed close the plan. A hero named Ruby runs through the chapter titles from trouble to rise in life. The tale itself is missing from this record.
the-little-lady-of-the-big-house:
Jack London's The Little Lady of the Big House opens with rancher Dick Forrest waking in the dark on his sleeping-porch. Forrest knows himself at once, master of broad acres, and listens with pleasure to the distant bawl of King Polo, his champion Short Horn bull. He plans new triumphs for the bull on the Eastern livestock circuits, meaning to prove that a California-born animal can beat corn-fed Iowa stock and imported bulls alike.

Rows of electric buttons beside his bed light the porch, a clock, a barometer, and thermometers. London builds the scene around wealth, machinery, and exact control of a great ranch. Readers meet a confident, rich cattleman at the height of his powers before the little lady of the title enters his ordered world.
the-lost-house:
Richard Harding Davis opens The Lost House on a dull day at the American chancellery in London. The ambassador is in Scotland unveiling a bust of Bobby Burns, the First Secretary watches a sham battle at Aldershot, and the attachés are at a football match and a pheasant shoot. The Second Secretary, alone, has just confided a state secret to his friend Austin Ford, the London correspondent of the New York Republic. Ford promises to cable it disguised as news from a Hungarian diplomat en route to Patagonia.

He really came, though, to ask about an international polo match. The Secretary begins a lecture: polo is a proposition of ponies, since men can be trained but ponies must be born. A page then interrupts with a visitor carrying an important note for the ambassador.
the-love-chase: James Sheridan Knowles wrote The Love-Chase, issued by Cassell and Company in London in 1887. Only the title page, the cast list, and the first stage direction are present here, so the comedy itself does not appear. The cast list preserves the original Haymarket performance of 1837, naming the actors: Mr. Strickland as Sir William Fondlove, Mr. Elton as Waller, who loves Lydia, Mr. Webster as the sportsman Wildrake, and Mrs. Glover as Widow Green. The scene is London, and act one opens in the lobby of an inn.
the-man-who-could-not-lose:
Richard Harding Davis's The Man Who Could Not Lose opens on a marriage made in haste that refused to repent at leisure. Champ Carter and his wife are so in love that they count the marriage their greatest asset; their friends count it the only thing against either of them. Champ, raised rich, was left by his father's death with no money and a few debts of honor. He has been paying them off ever since Yale by living on his pen, writing slowly for slow editors. Dolly Ingram's trouble is her mother, a leader of terrifying exclusiveness.

Widowed with millions to dispose of as she pleased, Mrs. Ingram keeps one ambition unfulfilled: to marry Dolly to an English duke. She has a shopworn duke, a bankrupt duke, and a young one in training.
the-maternal-management-of-children-in-h:
Thomas Bull, a London physician and lecturer on midwifery and the diseases of women and children, published The Maternal Management of Children, in Health and Disease in 1840. His preface addresses the young and inexperienced mother directly. Bull says such mothers almost never possess the knowledge his experience shows they need. Ignorance, he warns, has injured many infants' constitutions and cost some their lives.

The opening chapters cover the general management of the child in health. Bull teaches that prevention of disease is the mother's province, not its cure. He warns her never to tamper with medicine once illness has actually begun. A later chapter shows parents how to detect the first symptoms of disease early. Readers get a Victorian doctor's plain rules for nurseries, written before modern pediatrics existed.
the-mistress-of-the-manse:
J. G. Holland's The Mistress of the Manse, published in New York by Scribner, Armstrong and Co. in 1874, is a story told in verse. A short contents page names a prelude and three movements: Love's Experiments, Love's Philosophies, and Love's Consummations. The poem's shape is therefore a courtship and marriage followed through stages.

Love's Experiments opens as a crowd leaves a gate and a dusty coach draws up. The pastor and his bride step out and pass through a waiting door that closes on the watching street. Philip can only cry his wife's name, and Mildred answers that she is home, the old life closed and the new before them. Inside, the maid Dinah announces the mistress of the house.
the-new-adam-and-eve-from-mosses-from-an:
Nathaniel Hawthorne's tale The New Adam and Eve imagines the human race swept away while everything people made remains standing. The Day of Doom, following Father Miller's reading of prophecy, empties cities, fields, and islands of every living thing. Houses, tools, and all the footprints of human work stay untouched. A new Adam and a new Eve, created grown in mind and heart but knowing nothing of their predecessors, inherit the deserted earth.

Hawthorne proposes, half sportive and half thoughtful, to follow the pair through their first day. Such innocents, he argues, would at once tell art from nature, finding wisdom and simplicity in the one and elaborate puzzles in the other. Dawn comes with no human eye to see the east blush.
the-odyssey-rendered-into-english-prose-: Homer's Odyssey is rendered into English prose for readers who cannot read the original Greek. Only the front matter is present here, together with the start of a preface, so the epic itself does not appear. A dedication in Italian thanks Professor Biagio Ingroia as a precious ally. The contents list prefaces to two editions, all twenty-four books, and footnotes. The preface begins by saying the translation was meant to supplement another work, though the sentence breaks off.
the-old-manor-house:
Charlotte Smith published the novel The Old Manor House in 1793, in two volumes of numbered chapters. The pages present here give a life of the author before the contents. Charlotte Turner Smith was born in London in 1749, married at fifteen to pay her father's gambling debts, and endured a violent, wasteful husband.

Her life shaped her writing. She wrote Elegiac Sonnets in 1784 while living with her husband in a debtors' prison, and the book's success freed them. Her first novel, Emmeline, came in 1788, followed by nine more. A family inheritance stayed tied up in lawsuits for forty years, and she died in 1806 after years of debt and illness.
the-old-manse-from-mosses-from-an-old-ma:
Nathaniel Hawthorne introduces readers to his home in The Old Manse, the opening piece of Mosses from an Old Manse. He describes a gray old parsonage at the end of an avenue of black-ash trees, its gate long fallen from its hinges. A year has passed since the funeral of the aged clergyman who last lived there.

Hawthorne notes that no layman had lived in the house before him. A priest built it, priests followed, and the last minister alone wrote nearly three thousand sermons there. The new tenant, ashamed of his idle tales, hopes wisdom will fall on him with the leaves of the avenue.
the-old-stone-house:
Anne March, the pen name of Constance Fenimore Woolson, wrote The Old Stone House. The contents list eleven chapters, from The Five Cousins to a conclusion. Chapter One opens on Aunt Faith's birthday, the first of June, as she sits alone on the piazza looking back over more than fifty years.

Aunt Faith lost her husband while still a bride, then lost her brothers and sisters one by one. She became sole guardian of their five orphan children: Hugh and Sibyl Warrington, Tom and Grace Morris, and wild little Bessie Darrell from the southern hill country. For ten years she has watched over the band, and the novel follows life in her old stone house.
the-purchase-price-or-the-cause-of-compr: Emerson Hough, already known for The Mississippi Bubble and 54-40 or Fight, published his novel in 1910 with illustrations by M. Leone Bracker and Edmund Frederick, dedicating it to Senator Albert J. Beveridge. Twenty-three chapters move from a lady in company and a gateway scene through Tallwoods, an invasion, and an argument toward a payment and a Washington close. Only the title pages, dedication, and full chapter list are present here, so the narrative itself does not appear.
the-purse:
Honore de Balzac's short tale appears here in Clara Bell's English translation, dedicated to Sofka with a note on the family likeness medieval artists gave to paired figures in adoration. The story opens at twilight, an hour Balzac treats as made for artists and dreaming.

In that softened light a young painter stands back from his work and judges it with fresh eyes, as illusion loosens the grip of daily life. Balzac lingers on how half-light changes pictures, flesh, and fabric before any plot begins. Readers who enjoy his Parisian scenes will find atmosphere and artistic ambition carrying the opening.
the-rainbow-and-the-rose: E. Nesbit's poems of 1905, dedicated to Iris and Rosamund, are grouped in three parts. Headings in the first group speak of things that matter, confession, work, a jilted lover, and a beatific vision, while the second brings mummy wheat, a beech tree, absence, silence, and parting. Only the title pages and contents list are present here, so the poems themselves do not appear.
the-real-mother-goose: Nursery rhymes are gathered under Blanche Fisher Wright's illustrations in an edition dated 1916. A list of rhymes names Little Bo-Peep, Little Boy Blue, Pat-a-Cake, Jack, Solomon Grundy, and many other familiar figures, along with short pieces on rain, clocks, winter, and fingers and toes. Here only the title page and opening of the rhyme list are present, so the rhymes themselves do not appear.
the-secret-rose:
W. B. Yeats dedicated The Secret Rose to A. E. Its contents list the title piece and a dedication poem. Stories follow, including The Crucifixion of the Outcast and The Wisdom of the King. Where There Is Nothing, There Is God is also named. A long tale of Costello the Proud closes the list. Two epigraphs from Villiers de L'Isle Adam and Leonardo da Vinci precede the dedication.

In his letter to A. E., Yeats says the stories share one subject. It is the war of spiritual with natural order, he writes. He wrote them at different times and in different manners, without a definite plan. Irish friends ask when he will write a really national romance, he adds. He answers that poetry comes from looking into the self. That little, infinite, faltering, eternal flame is his source, not famous moments of history.
the-servant-in-the-house: Charles Rann Kennedy's play The Servant in the House is dated 1908 in the front matter shown. Kennedy dedicated it to Walter Hampden. Long quotations from the First Epistle of John follow it. They warn that a man who hates his brother walks in darkness. George Frederick Watts is quoted on the hunger for brotherhood lying beneath modern unrest. The portion shown ends at the heading for the original cast of characters, so no cast or dialogue appears.
the-silent-house: Fergus Hume's The Silent House was published in New York by C. H. Doscher, who held its 1907 copyright. The pages shown give the title matter and contents only. No chapter text follows. The tenant of the silent house opens the list. Shadows on the blind and an unsatisfactory explanation come next. Mrs. Vrain's story and the assurance money follow partway through. Gossip appears at chapter thirteen, where the shown list ends.
the-song-book-of-quong-lee-of-limehouse: Thomas Burke's song book gathers short verses spoken in the voice of Quong Lee of Limehouse, London's old Chinese quarter. Here only the title page and contents have come down. The list runs from Buying and Selling and The Power of Music through pieces on shop windows, lanterns, and tea making. Politicians, gambling, and the Great White War also get their verses, so the poems themselves do not appear.
the-story-of-a-white-rocking-horse: Laura Lee Hope's Make Believe story of a white rocking horse, illustrated by Harry L. Smith, is presented here through its title pages and publisher's lists alone. Those lists place the book among the Make Believe stories. The Sawdust Doll, the Lamb on Wheels, and the Bold Tin Soldier stand beside it. Long Bobbsey Twins and Bunny Brown lists then open. The rocking horse's own adventures do not appear.
the-tale-of-dickie-deer-mouse: Arthur Scott Bailey's animal tale was published by Grosset and Dunlap in 1918, illustrated by Diane Petersen. Only the title pages and a contents list appear in this record. The contents show twelve chapters. A little gentleman hunts a home in them. He meets a startled sleeper and a blackbird's nest. He takes a summer home. He visits the cornfield. He helps Fatty Coon. Dickie Deer Mouse's own adventures do not appear.
the-tale-of-mrs-tittlemouse: Beatrix Potter's Mrs. Tittlemouse was first published by Frederick Warne in 1910, and this record shows a 1985 Penguin impression. The pages present give the title, the publisher's details, and just the first line of the tale, which introduces a wood-mouse named Mrs. Tittlemouse. Her tidy little house, her unwanted visitors, and the spring cleaning that fill the famous story lie beyond what is shown here. Readers get the book's identity and its opening breath, and no more.
the-uninhabited-house:
Charlotte Riddell, an Irish writer of ghost tales, wrote this short tale of a haunted house in 1875. She was the most calm and sure hand at the ghost tale of her age in Britain. Her tale deals with a house no tenant will keep, on a river bank.

A clerk in a law office is paid to lodge in River Hall and break its ill name. By patience and a cool head he works out the fraud and dread that hang on the house. The tale is the quiet peak of the Victorian ghost tale, free of all cheap shock.
the-white-linen-nurse:
Eleanor Hallowell Abbott published The White Linen Nurse in 1913, dedicating the little story to Maurice Howe Richardson, who loved romance almost as much as surgery. Chapter one finds the nurse so tired that her noble expression aches. Her head, shoulders, lungs, and ankle-bones ache too, but only the expression feels permanently damaged by three ether-scented years of hospital training.

She studies her bright Nova Scotian reflection in the prim white mirror over her bureau. The face is perfectly good and tidy, she judges, except that it looks disgustingly noble, hygienic, and dollish. Her conscientious sickroom smile hangs like lip-coloured lead from her nose. Abbott opens a romance with its heroine rebelling against her own saintly mask.
the-wise-mamma-goose:
Charlotte B. Herr wrote The Wise Mamma Goose, a children's story published in 1913 with designs by Frances Beem. The book opens with a blank space for a child's name. Mamma Goose has slipped away from a noisy barnyard to think. She hides between tall red hollyhocks in the garden. Thinking, readers learn, has always been hard work for her.

Twelve goslings keep her busy every day. They are soft, round, and fluffy like little yellow balls. Herr compares them proudly with Red Hen's chicks. The goslings find their own breakfasts and love the water. Young readers get a gentle farmyard tale told with warm humor.
the-wooden-horse: Hugh Walpole's The Wooden Horse is shown only through its publication pages in this record. Macmillan first published the novel in April 1909. A new edition followed in 1919, with a portrait of the author. Impressions and a Wayfarers' Library issue came between. No chapter or line of the story itself appears in the pages present here.
theocritus-bion-and-moschus-rendered-int: Andrew Lang rendered the Greek pastoral poets Theocritus, Bion, and Moschus into English prose for Macmillan in 1889. Lang, lately a fellow of Merton College, Oxford, added an introductory essay. The volume is dedicated to Ernest Myers. A contents page lists the essay on Theocritus and his age, then the idyls in order. In this record the listing is where things stop, so Lang's prose versions themselves are not shown.
this-side-of-paradise:
F. Scott Fitzgerald's novel follows Amory Blaine through two books, The Romantic Egotist and The Education of a Personage. Quotations from Rupert Brooke and Oscar Wilde open the volume, which Fitzgerald dedicated to Sigourney Fay. An interlude covers May 1917 to February 1919.

Chapter one presents Amory's parents, Stephen and Beatrice Blaine. Stephen, a Byron-loving man who dozed over encyclopedias, grew rich through two brothers' deaths and met Beatrice at Bar Harbor. Amory inherits his mother's traits and his father's height and wavering. Readers get a debut novel about privilege, romance, and self-invention.
trent-s-last-case: E. C. Bentley dedicates Trent's Last Case, subtitled The Woman in Black, to G. K. Chesterton in a long letter. He owes Chesterton a book in return for The Man Who Was Thursday, he writes. He also unfolded the story's plan to him two years earlier, surrounded by Frenchmen. The contents promise chapters from Bad News and The Inquest to Eruption and Writing a Letter. Only the dedication and contents are present here, so the detective story itself does not appear.
vignettes-in-verse:
Matilda Betham published Vignettes in Verse in 1818. She inscribed the poems to Lady Betham, in respect for her amiable qualities. Her advertisement, dated at Stonkam on May 10 of that year, explains an odd delay. Most of the poems had been printed some two years before. Events seemed set to keep them from ever appearing. Only now has she found the rest of the manuscript.

Reading the whole over, Betham says, struck her with surprise. The verses now look prophetic. She wrote them with a vague, general view. Yet they seem to speak of what has since befallen her: a long seclusion, cut off from the common means of study. That loss gave rise to a pursuit that now fills her life. The first poem plays with journals and wings, each pair of wings a day. Grief and foresight haunt these short pieces from the start.
whitefoot-the-wood-mouse:
Thornton W. Burgess wrote Whitefoot the Wood Mouse, a nature tale for children. Chapter one finds Whitefoot at the end of his happiest winter yet. Whitefoot never lets past troubles spoil the present, Burgess says. He also never borrows worry from the future. That habit keeps him cheerful in a risky life.

Few creatures in the Green Forest face more foes than this small mouse. Buster Bear, Billy Mink, Shadow the Weasel, and Hooty the Owl all hunt him. Foxes and Old Man Coyote watch for him too. He must be ready to run at any moment. Burgess turns wood lore into warm tales of the small and quick.
willie-mouse:
Alta Tabor wrote Willie Mouse, a picture tale for young children from the Saalfield company. Willie Mouse had often heard his mother and father say the moon was made of green cheese. One evening he set out to see if he could find it. The subtitle calls the trip a journey to find the moon.

Willie packs some cheese and a bread crust for the road. He takes his lantern and starts his travels at night. Pictures break up the short lines of text. Tabor gives small readers a gentle quest built on a child's literal belief. A mouse, a lantern, and green cheese carry the tale.
wise-or-otherwise: The pages present here hold title pages and an empty contents heading for Wise or Otherwise, by Lydia Leavitt and Thad. W. H. Leavitt, with no tales shown. The Wells company printed the book in Toronto in 1898. Anna Lake drew the pictures. Lydia Leavitt also wrote Bohemian Society and A Trip Around the World. Her co-author wrote The Witch of Plum Hollow and tales of the gold fields. The book was entered at the Department of Agriculture in 1898, by its copyright line.
words-for-the-wise:
T. S. Arthur published these moral tales in Philadelphia in 1851. His short preface hopes the lessons will warn and guide many readers. The contents promise stories about a poor debtor, a Sunday Christian, and a man who could not get along. Other tales warn against haste to grow rich and against taking things for granted.

The opening story begins with a rich merchant praising one honest man. That man is Moale, a tailor. Each tale turns a small daily failing into a clear lesson. Arthur writes for household readers who want fiction with direct moral use.
zizhi-tongjian-sima-guang-chinese:
Sima Guang, a statesman of the Song court, led a team that spent nineteen years building the Zizhi Tongjian, finished in 1084 CE. Its title means a mirror for aid in ruling. The text here is the complete work, 294 chapters in classical Chinese, from Chinese Wikisource.

Year by year the mirror runs from the Warring States in 403 BCE to the Five Dynasties in 959 CE. Sima Guang chose events for the lessons they taught rulers, and he weighed his sources in open notes. The work is the great year-by-year history of imperial China. Statesmen read it for a thousand years as a handbook of rule.
